SAVE - Suicide Awareness Voices of Education

list.listitem: 50-65% of completed adult suicides visited a physician in the month prior to death and 10-40% in the week prior to the suicide, and 90% of those who die by suicide have a psychiatric illness at the time of death (can be diagnosed, undiagnosed or misdiagnosed). C

Risk of self-harm increases with psychiatric illness, recent loss or personal crisis, chronic illness, substance use/abuse, and prior episodes of self harm. Greatest risk occurs within the first 60 days following discharge from a hospital or ER visit. B

Ask about current intent, method and means, and active preparations, risk and protective factors present. Treat underlying contributors to self-harm with cognitively oriented psychotherapy and medication as appropriate. C

background.definition: Suicidal self-directed violence is defined as behavior that is self-directed and deliberately results in injury or the potential for injury to oneself. There is evidence, whether implicit or explicit, of suicidal intent.

list.listitem: There are approximately 45,000 deaths from suicide each year.
There is one completed suicide for every 25 attempted suicides.
In the United States there are approximately 1.3 million attempts each year, corresponding to one attempt made every 28 seconds.
The age-adjusted rate is 14.7 suicides per 100,000 persons in the United States.

For suicide, the male to female ratio is 4:1 for completed suicides. Rates vary by race: Caucasian 14.1/100,000; non-white 5.8/100,000. Suicide is more common among elderly than the young (14.9/100,000/year among 65 + years, compared with 10.5/100,000 among 15 to 24).
Females, in comparison to males, attempt suicide more at a rate of 3:1
There is an increased prevalence of attempts for youth, American Indians and LGBTQ orientation.
Female physicians have a higher standardized mortality ratio (SMR) for suicide compared to women in general; conversely, male physicians have a lower SMR for suicide compared to men in general.
Suicides and self-harm injury cost society about $70 billion in combined medical and work loss costs.
Suicide is the 10th leading cause of death in the United States, and 5th leading cause of potential life years lost, and is the cause of 1.6% of all US deaths.
There is no single etiology; rather, it is multi-faceted. There may be a triggering event, but there are always multiple underlying causes to suicide.
In completed suicides, there is a wide range of methods employed which differ considerably by gender, age, and ethnicity; access to lethal means, geography.

Etiological factors include mood and psychotic disorders, substance use disorders (especially in combination with depressive or mood disorders), some personality disorders and chronic medical illness.

A study of active duty soldiers found that the strongest predictors of completed suicide after hospital discharge for a psychiatric disorder were male sex (OR 7.9), lage age at enlistment (OR 1.9), weapens possession (OR 5.6), prior suicidality (OR 2.9), and a greater number of diagnoses and prescriptions for depression.
Suicide deaths were associated with having opioid prescriptions, especially high-dose or having 3 or more prescribers.
A systematic review found no evidence to support an association between GLP-1 RA treatment and suicide or self-harm events in adults with diabetes, overweight, or obesity.
No single biological pathogen or physiological process accounts for suicidal ideation and related behaviors.
Multiple sources are contributory, including mood disorders, chronic illness, situational crises, and substance intoxication, as well as prescription drug addiction.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history of attempts or completed suicide

list.listitem: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2023) recommends screening for depression, but found that the evidence was insufficient to recommend for or against screening for suicide risk.C
A previous suicide attempt is the strongest predictor for future suicide attempts; 60% of completed suicides occur on the first (and only) attempt. B
USPSTF gives an I recommendation for "Insufficient Evidence" regarding the potential benefits and harms of screening for suicde risk during routine visits.
Similarly, VA/DOD guidelines do not recommend screening the general public for suicide risk, and instead focusing on case-finding by identifying persons with warning signs for suicide.
Case-finding is highly recommended for patients with depression, chronic illness, recent loss, or other psychiatric illness.
The best evaluated screening test has 100% sensitivity, 81% specificity, but due to the very low prevalence of suicide in the population, had only a 6% positive predictive value.
A poster is available that can be used to raise awareness in healthcare settings but has not been well studied.
A Cochrane review concluded that university based interventions to prevent suicide increased knowledge but had an uncertain effect on suicidal behaviors.
Restricting access to lethal means of harm does appear to be effective, as are school-based awareness programs.

A brief suicide prevention intervention delivered in a single in-person encounter is associated with reduced subsequent attempts (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53-0.89) and increased linkage to follow-up (OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.8 - 5.2) but had no effect on depression symptoms.

Downloadable phone applications for depression and suicide prevention management are not extensively governed, may provide inaccurate helpline phone numbers, and do not routinely use all six evidence-based suicide prevention strategies.
Suicidal ideation and deliberate self harm are considered symptoms of psychiatric illness, personal crisis, or disordered thinking rather than a disease diagnosis. C
Ask about current intent (vs. vague ideation), obtaining means (pills, firearm), and preparations underway (looking for ways to die, researching suicide online). C

Risk is increased with a clear plan and intent, psychiatric illness (depression, bipolar or borderline personality disorder), recent loss or crisis, chronic illness, substance use/abuse, prior episodes of self harm. C
Previous deliberate self harm increases the risk for future self-harm events and completed suicide.
Ask patients about access to weapons and potentially harmful prescribed or illicit drugs.

Patients present with a broad spectrum of thoughts and behaviors, from vague suicidal thoughts, overall sense of hopelessness, despair, a sense of burdensomeness, mature and specific plans, or previous attempts.

About 2 to 3% of primary care patients have experienced suicidal ideation in the last month, often vague in plan and with strong ambivalence of intention. Approximately 50 to 65% of completed adult suicides visited a physician in the month prior to death, and 10 to 40% visited a physician in the week prior to the completed suicide. A study in 443 adults in general practices in London confirmed that asking about suicide does not trigger suicidal ideation.

A study of active duty soldiers found that the strongest predictors of completed suicide after hospital discharge for a psychiatric disorder were male sex (OR 7.9), lage age at enlistment (OR 1.9), weapens possession (OR 5.6), prior suicidality (OR 2.9), and a greater number of diagnoses and prescriptions for depression.

In a study of suicide risk assessment in secondary mental healthcare, hopelessness (RR 2.2) and having experienced a significant loss (RR 1.9) were the strongest independent predictors. Among patients who made a suicide attempt, those who made definite plans and made extensive preparations were at increased risk for subsequent attempts.

Approximately 90% of those who die by suicide have a psychiatric illness at the time of death (can be diagnosed, undiagnosed or misdiagnosed). However, many people who died by suicide did not have a known mental health condition, highlighting the fact that the absence of mental health disorders does not eliminate the risk for suicide. If a primary care clinician is in doubt about levels of risk and strategies for management, additional assessment and involvement of a behavioral health provider is strongly recommended.
Among adolescents, there a meta-analysis found strong associations between depressive disorders, anxiety disorders, and suicide attempts.
A validated clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of suicidal ideation based on mood disturbance, sleep disturbance, guilt, and hopelessness.
Another validated clinical decision rule can be used to predict the likelihood of a repeated attempt in patients presenting with a suicide attempt.

Ask about specific suicidal ideation: frequency, intensity, specificity, and nature, and whether the patient has decided on a method, developed plans for the act, or obtained the means to carry it out.

Assess for psychiatric illnesses associated with self-harm and suicidal behavior: depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, borderline personality, chronic illness, and substance intoxication/abuse.
Assess psychosocial contributors to risk, such as recent losses, employment, financial or legal difficulties, suicide or attempts in other family members.
Assess current situational and psychosocial supports: family, friends, co-workers, neighbors, health care providers who know and care for the patient.
Treat underlying contributors with cognitively oriented psychotherapy (e.g. problem solving therapy, CBT, dialectical behavior therapy) and psychotropic medication.B
Provide a way to contact provider and local or national hot-lines for suicide. C
Hospitalize if attempt is imminent or risk of suicide is deemed high.B
If patient is a danger to self, involuntary hospitalization can be imposed by the physician (laws vary by state). C

SSRIs and SSNRIs can reduce depressive symptoms if depression is a contributing factor to the suicidal ideation. A Cochrane review found only limited clinical trial evidence regarding prevention of deliberate self-harm and suicide, including antidepressants.
Lithium salts have been shown to reduce suicidal thoughts and attempts in patients with bipolar disorder.

A systematic review identified 9 RCTs of esketamine nasal spray in patients with major depressive disorder. Based on small studies, it seems to quickly reduce suicidal ideation in patients with depression. It may induce remission of symptoms in patients with moderate to severe depression who have not responded to other treatments. Side effects are common.
Anti-anxiety agents can reduce agitation and anxiety in patients with high level of distress and suicidal intent.

Because drug overdose is a common method of suicide attempt and completion, care should be exercised in evaluating the toxicity of any prescription medication provided, and amounts dispensed should be less than a lethal dose.

In 2004 the FDA issues Black Box Warning Label for antidepressants for youth (under 18) and in 2006 for young adults (19-25). Advise patients and family of increased risk of suicidal ideation prior to prescribing and ensure routine follow-up with patients during initial 6 weeks of medication administration.

A study that linked a primary care database with prescriptions found that the risk of suicide or self-harm varied depending on the drug prescribed, even after adjusting for differences between patients using propensity scoring. Within class, there was little difference between SSRIs and tricyclics, but suicide rates were significantly increased with mirtazapine and venlafaxine (HR 3.7 and 2.2 compared with citalopram).
Cognitive behavioral therapy and dialectical behavior therapy are endorsed after the acute risk of suicide has passed by the VA/DOD guidelines.

Cognitive-based psychotherapies have been shown to reduce repeat attempts. For example, an RCT in active duty personnel at risk for suicide (previous attempt or ideation) found a significantly reduced risk of suicide attempt in those randomized to brief CBT (14% vs. 40%, NNT = 4).

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has been shown to reduce episodes of deliberate self harm in patients with borderline personality disorder. In a randomized trial, 99 women with borderline personality disorder and at least two attempts or acts of self-injury were randomized to three kinds of DBT which had similar effects. DBT that included skills training made it more effective.
An RCT with 84 patients also found that a brief DBT intervention was effective compared to waitlisted controls.
An ongoing therapeutic alliance with a primary care or behavioral health provider and good aftercare may reduce the risk of repeated self-harm.
Research on follow-up care with patients demonstrates a reduced risk of suicide immediately following hospitalization in those patients receiving continued care.

Crisis response plans (CRP) are reduce suicidal behaviors in suicidal patients. A study comparing a standard CRP with a CRP enhanced by providing reasons for living and with treatment as usual found that both CRPs were acceptable. More frequent use of the enhanced CRP was associated with less suicidal ideation.

Acceptance and commitment therapy uses mindfulness and acceptance strategies, coupled with commitment and behavior change strategies. A small RCT (n = 40) found improvements in the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale compared with a relaxation control group.
Refer patient to appropriate services to support management of underlying psychosocial loss or crisis, such as unemployment and financial difficulties.

Patients assessed to be at high risk of suicide (and many at moderate risk) such as those with current suicidal intent, a mature plan, acquisition of means to commit suicide, and/or undergoing preparations to carry out the plan should be considered for immediate hospitalization.
Patients who pose a danger to self (or others) can be hospitalized involuntarily for brief periods (72 hours, state laws vary).
Prognosis is thought to be better if there is no prior attempt, if the patient has multiple protective factors and support systems available, and if follow-up care is provided. C
The likelihood of completed suicide is higher when patients have depression or schizophrenia.B

Completed suicides are a rare event, but ideation and self-harm behaviors can be chronic and repetitive. While there is no accurate instrument for predicting who will actually complete a lethal suicide attempt, assessing risk factors by demographics or levels of distress and intention can help practitioners decide on an appropriate level of response. In addition, when available external sources of information (in particular spouse, family, etc.) can provide helpful information in determining plans.
Better prognosis if the provider and patient have an ongoing therapeutic alliance.
Monitoring of suicidal ideation and risk factors should take place in the context of an ongoing therapeutic alliance with a consistent behavioral health provider or primary care provider.
Focus of therapeutic intervention should be on factors that are changeable, such as thought processes, mood, and levels of psychosocial support, opportunities and future.

Depression and life events can make life seem hopeless at times. This can affect how you think about your future and options for your life. Please make a commitment with me now NOT to make a life ending decision while you are feeling so overwhelmed.
Many people consider ending their lives when they feel depressed, in pain, and/or are overwhelmed. It is very important to talk about those thoughts and feelings with someone you trust who can help.

When people think seriously about suicide, most have strong feelings of ambivalence (part of them wants to, part of them doesn't). It is very important that we can talk about both sides of this issue in your life.
Elderly people are less like to complain of depression and ideation, but more likely to make serious or completed attempt.
The highest rates of suicide in the US are among white male, elderly, widowed or divorced, urban residents living alone.

Treatment principles are the same for elderly as for other age groups, with special attention to higher rates of depression, frequency of losses, isolation, physical limitations and/or impairments and a sense of no future among the elderly driving hopelessness and suicidal ideation.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends asking about mood disorders, sexual orientation, suicidal thoughts during routine healthcare visits.

Adolescent suicidality (ideation, behavior, or both) is common in the United States, and homicide remains one of the leading causes of death for young people aged 10 to 24 years. Attempts have been made to develop an algorithm and validated screening tool for emergency department assessment of risk of violence to self and others in adolescents.
